about: Learning catalog of the web UI. Topic ids are stable: fields and pages refer to them (placements), and a future Tech Basics site can be linked by replacing a topic's links or destination without changing the application. destination.type 'internal' shows the explanation inside the app; links point to official documentation.

topics.title: PowerShell
topics.summary: The command shell built into Windows. This tool's scripts (install.ps1, webui.ps1, services.ps1) are PowerShell scripts; you start them with powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\script.ps1.

topics.title: Windows Terminal
topics.summary: A modern window for PowerShell and other shells, with tabs. Any terminal works for running these scripts.

topics.title: Changing directories and file paths
topics.summary: cd C:\path\to\folder moves into a folder; .\ means the current folder. Paths with spaces need quotes: cd "C:\Users\you\My Projects".

topics.title: Environment variables
topics.summary: Named values such as %USERPROFILE% (your profile folder) used by programs. In PowerShell they are written $env:USERPROFILE.

topics.title: Reading command output
topics.summary: Scripts print what they check and change. Lines starting with WARNING need attention; red text is an error that stopped the script. The technical output sections in this app show the same text.

topics.title: Shell navigation
topics.summary: Containers run Linux. ls lists files, cd changes folders, cat shows a file. docker exec -it <container> sh opens a shell inside a container.

links.title: The Linux command line for beginners (Ubuntu)

topics.title: Permissions
topics.summary: Files have an owner, a group and read/write/execute bits (chmod, chown). The containers here run read-only with dropped capabilities.

topics.title: Processes
topics.summary: Each container runs one main process. If it exits, the container stops; Docker restarts it when the restart policy says so.

topics.title: Editing configuration files
topics.summary: Generated files (svc-*.yml, admin-dashboard.yml) are overwritten by this tool; put hand-written Traefik configuration in another .yml file in traefik\dynamic.

topics.title: Reading logs
topics.summary: docker logs <container> shows a container's output. Traefik marks problems with WRN or ERR; cloudflared reports registered tunnel connections.

topics.title: SSH
topics.summary: An encrypted remote shell. Not needed here: this tool and its web UI run locally on the Windows PC.

topics.title: What a repository is
topics.summary: A folder of source files plus its full history. This tool is a repository: the scripts you run come from it, while your instance's settings live in the separate install folder.

topics.title: Clone, commit, branch and pull
topics.summary: git clone copies a repository, git pull updates it, git checkout <branch> switches versions. Commits are saved snapshots.

topics.title: Source code versus running software
topics.summary: Updating the repository does not change what runs. install.ps1 copies the new version into the install folder; containers change only when you start or restart them.

topics.title: Updating this project
topics.summary: Back up (Backups page), pull the new version, run install.ps1 -DryRun to see the changes, then install.ps1 without -Start. Your settings, services and Cloudflare configuration are kept.

topics.title: Releases
topics.summary: A release is a named, tested version (a tag). Prefer releases over arbitrary branches for your live installation.

topics.title: Containers
topics.summary: A container is an isolated program with everything it needs. This tool runs three: Traefik (the router), a Docker socket proxy (lets Traefik read container names safely) and cloudflared (the tunnel connector).

topics.title: Images
topics.summary: An image is the read-only template a container starts from. Images here are pinned by version and digest, so updates are deliberate.

topics.title: Docker Compose
topics.summary: compose.yaml describes the containers of this instance; docker compose up starts exactly those, named after the instance.

topics.title: Volumes and bind mounts
topics.summary: Folders shared into a container. Traefik reads traefik\dynamic from the install folder read-only.

topics.title: Port publishing
topics.summary: A published port lets programs on the PC reach a container. Traefik's two ports are published on 127.0.0.1 only, so other devices on your network cannot reach them.

topics.title: Docker networks
topics.summary: Containers on the same user-defined network can talk to each other. Apps you publish join the shared proxy network; cloudflared sits on a separate small network with a fixed address, the only one Traefik trusts for forwarded headers.

topics.title: Container DNS names
topics.summary: On a shared user-defined network, a container is reachable by its name, for example http://uptime-kuma:3001. Prefer names to container IP addresses, which change when containers are recreated.

topics.title: Docker Desktop versus Docker Engine
topics.summary: Docker Desktop runs Docker Engine inside a small Linux VM (WSL 2) on Windows and adds a tray app. It must run in Linux containers mode. Programs on Windows are reached from containers as host.docker.internal.

topics.title: IPv4 addresses
topics.summary: Four numbers like 10.20.30.11 identify a device on a network. A port number (like 4119) then selects a program on that device.

topics.title: Private addresses (RFC 1918)
topics.summary: 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x and 192.168.x.x are private: used inside homes and offices, never routed on the Internet.

topics.title: Subnets and CIDR notation
topics.summary: 172.31.250.0/28 means the 16 addresses 172.31.250.0-15. The tunnel network must not overlap any other Docker network; Suggest free values picks one that doesn't.

topics.title: LAN versus WAN
topics.summary: The LAN is your home or office network; the WAN is the Internet side of your router. With a Cloudflare Tunnel, nothing on the WAN side is opened.

topics.title: DNS resolution
topics.summary: DNS turns a name like mediabox.example.com into an address. Public DNS (Cloudflare) answers for the Internet; a local resolver such as Pi-hole can answer differently inside your network.

topics.title: Ports and protocols
topics.summary: Web apps speak HTTP (or HTTPS) on a TCP port. Cloudflare's HTTP tunnel publishing carries HTTP(S) and WebSockets; arbitrary TCP or UDP services are not published by this tool.

topics.title: NAT and port forwarding
topics.summary: Port forwarding on a router sends Internet traffic to a device inside. A Cloudflare Tunnel makes it unnecessary because the connection is made outbound from this PC.

topics.title: Reverse proxies
topics.summary: A reverse proxy receives requests for many hostnames on one entry point and forwards each to the right app. Traefik is the reverse proxy here.

topics.title: HTTPS and TLS
topics.summary: HTTPS encrypts traffic between the browser and the server holding the certificate. With a tunnel, Cloudflare holds the certificate at its edge and the tunnel to this PC is encrypted separately.

topics.title: A and AAAA records
topics.summary: An A record points a name at an IPv4 address (AAAA: IPv6). Used for public-IP ingress; this tool never changes A/AAAA records automatically.

topics.title: CNAME records
topics.summary: A CNAME makes a name an alias of another. Each published hostname gets a proxied CNAME to <tunnel-id>.cfargotunnel.com.

topics.title: MX and TXT records
topics.summary: MX records route email; TXT records hold SPF, DKIM, DMARC and verification values. This tool never touches them.

topics.title: TTL
topics.summary: How long resolvers may cache an answer. Proxied Cloudflare records use 'Auto'; a new record can still take a few minutes to be seen everywhere.

topics.title: FQDNs and subdomains
topics.summary: A fully qualified domain name such as mediabox.example.com: the subdomain (mediabox) plus a domain you own on Cloudflare (example.com).

topics.title: Internal versus external DNS
topics.summary: For local-only use, a resolver on your network (Pi-hole, your router) can point names like service.local.example.com at this PC's LAN address. Note that Traefik's ports here listen on 127.0.0.1 only.

topics.title: Zones and accounts
topics.summary: An account holds tunnels and Access settings (account-level permissions). Each domain in it is a zone with its own DNS (zone-level permissions). The token needs both kinds.

topics.title: API tokens
topics.summary: A token lets this tool make specific changes in your account, limited to the permissions and domains you choose. It is shown once by Cloudflare and stored here encrypted for your Windows account.

topics.title: Cloudflare Tunnel
topics.summary: An outbound, encrypted connection from this PC to Cloudflare. Requests for your hostnames travel down the tunnel, so no router port is opened. Many hostnames can share one tunnel.

topics.title: cloudflared
topics.summary: The connector program that keeps the tunnel open. It runs as this instance's cloudflared container and forwards every request to Traefik.

topics.title: Published application routes
topics.summary: Rules on the tunnel that say which hostname goes where. This tool sends every hostname to http://traefik:80; Traefik then picks the app.

topics.title: Cloudflare Access
topics.summary: A login in front of an app, enforced by Cloudflare before any request reaches your network. Only the emails you allow can sign in. Required for the public Traefik dashboard.

topics.title: DNS proxying
topics.summary: A proxied (orange-cloud) record sends visitors to Cloudflare, which then uses the tunnel. Tunnel hostnames must be proxied.

topics.title: SSL/TLS termination
topics.summary: Cloudflare issues and renews the HTTPS certificates for proxied hostnames at its edge. No Let's Encrypt account or ACME email is involved in tunnel mode.

topics.title: Routers
topics.summary: A router matches requests (for example Host(`mediabox.example.com`)) and hands them to a service. Each published service here has one generated router.

topics.title: Services
topics.summary: A Traefik service knows the backend address (for example http://10.20.30.11:4119).

topics.title: Middlewares
topics.summary: Steps applied to requests on the way, such as security headers (default-headers) or stripping a path prefix.

topics.title: Entry points
topics.summary: Ports Traefik listens on. web (:80 inside, published on 127.0.0.1) receives app traffic from cloudflared; traefik (:8080) serves the local dashboard and API.

topics.title: Docker discovery
topics.summary: Traefik can also read routes from container labels, through a read-only socket proxy. This tool mainly uses generated files instead.

topics.title: Hostname routing
topics.summary: All hostnames arrive at the same Traefik; it reads the requested name and forwards to the matching app.

topics.title: Path-prefix routing
topics.summary: https://example.com/mediabox sends only that path to an app. Many apps break unless they are configured for that base path; prefer a subdomain.

topics.title: Dashboard and API
topics.summary: Traefik's own read-only web page listing routers, services and middlewares. Always available on this PC; it can also be published behind Cloudflare Access as a first end-to-end test.

topics.title: 404, 502 and 504 errors
topics.summary: 404: no route matches the hostname (typo, service disabled). 502: the route exists but the app cannot be reached (wrong address or port, app stopped, firewall). 504/524: the app answered too slowly.

topics.title: Detail levels
topics.summary: Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced and Expert change how much is shown, never what is allowed or how changes are checked. Switch at any time from the top bar.

topics.title: Validated, reviewed, applied, healthy
topics.summary: Validated: the tool checked it. Reviewed: you looked at it (this changes nothing technical). Applied: the change was made. Healthy: a live check passed. A review is reset when the content changes.

topics.title: Backups and recovery points
topics.summary: Exports never contain your API token or tunnel token. Restores are previewed and approved in two parts (this PC, then Cloudflare). A recovery point is saved before every change.

topics.title: Instances
topics.summary: An instance is one Traefik + cloudflared stack with its own name, ports and networks. Several can run on one PC without interfering, each in its own install folder.

topics.title: Local-only installations
topics.summary: Without Cloudflare, Traefik routes hostnames on this PC (127.0.0.1). Test with curl -H "Host: app.example.com" http://127.0.0.1:8180/ or a hosts-file entry. A tunnel can be added later.

topics.title: Public-IP ingress (planned)
topics.summary: Not implemented in this version. It would need an A record to your WAN address, router/pfSense NAT on ports 80/443, Traefik certificates (Let's Encrypt) and WAN hardening. Use Cloudflare Tunnel instead.

topics.title: Other Traefik management tools
topics.summary: This tool deliberately covers deployment, basic service publishing, backups and troubleshooting. For middleware chains, certificates, load balancing or plugins, use Traefik's own configuration or a dedicated third-party manager as a separate product.

topics.title: Google audience: External or Internal
topics.summary: External lets any Google account (including ordinary @gmail.com accounts) sign in to your app; choose it unless everyone belongs to your own Google Workspace organization. Internal is only offered to Workspace (or Cloud Identity) organizations and limits sign-in to that organization. Either way, authentik still decides who may create an account and what they may open.

topics.title: Testing or In production
topics.summary: A new External app starts in Testing: only the test users you list (up to 100) can sign in, so add your own Google account as a test user. Publish app (In production) lets any Google account reach the Google sign-in screen. Publishing does not give anyone access to your applications: authentik's rules still decide that. Apps that only ask for openid, email and profile need no Google verification.

topics.title: Google branding
topics.summary: The app name and a support email are required; they appear on Google's consent screen. A logo, home page, privacy policy and terms links are optional: leave them empty (a logo starts Google's brand verification). The authorized domain is the domain of your sign-in address.

topics.title: Authorized redirect URI
topics.summary: The exact address Google sends people back to after they signed in: authentik's callback for the Google source. Google compares it character by character, including https, the host name and the trailing slash.

links.title: Google OAuth 2.0 for web server apps

topics.title: Client JSON file
topics.summary: After creating a Web application client, Google offers Download JSON. The file holds the client ID, the client secret and the redirect URIs. Import it here: the manager checks it and passes the secret to authentik once; it is not stored by the manager. Google shows and downloads the secret only right after the client (or a new secret) is created.

topics.title: Internal or External authentik account
topics.summary: authentik users are Internal (they can open authentik's own dashboard and application list) or External (only the applications, not the dashboard). The owner is created as an Internal user. This has nothing to do with Google's External audience.

topics.title: The DTC owners group
topics.summary: The initial access rule: protected applications that have no rule of their own in authentik admit the members of this group. The owner and akadmin are in it. Add people, or give applications other rules, in authentik.

topics.title: Local recovery sign-in
topics.summary: akadmin keeps its password and can always sign in on this PC at authentik's local address, even if Google or Cloudflare are unavailable. The original sign-in flow stays reachable at /if/flow/default-authentication-flow/.

topics.title: ForwardAuth
topics.summary: Traefik asks authentik, for every request to a protected application, whether the visitor is signed in and allowed. Unknown visitors are sent to the sign-in page; if authentik does not answer, Traefik refuses the request.
